Turkiye-Syria Earthquakes 2023

By: Chwayitisa Futshane | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
... in the aftermath of the devastating earthquakes in Turkiye and Syria, we take you inside the unfolding tragedy.

Unique Selling Point:
Turkey and Syria earthquake - the death toll passes 11,000.

Summary:
Opening:
Clips from social media, chaos, devastation, up-sounds…
VO:
In the early hours of Monday morning, multiple deadly earthquakes, rocked Syria and Türkiye.

It’s a tragedy that struck thousands of kms away. But, even here, in a suburban restaurant in Sunninghill Johannesburg, popular with locals and expats, the aftershocks are being felt...
Fatih:
When I woke up, I saw the news, tried to phone someone, they did not answer… I texted using whatsapp…
Maybe they died, maybe they are still alive, some of them.
VO:
Fatih grew up in Türkiye, but moved to Joburg to run his restaurant, Istanbul Kebab. Following the disaster, he was desperately trying to get hold of his family back home, but to no avail. Then, hours later, came the good news… they were unharmed.
Fatih:
I can't tell you, you have to be there, we can see what's happening there. We are sad for other people! They lose their family and everything, actually.
According to reports, 23 million people have been affected by these earthquakes. However, this is not a new phenomenon. Earthquakes are a common occurrence in the region.
Yashni:
It was a 7.7 Magnitude earthquake, that is massive. That happened in the early hours of the morning, just after 4 O'clock.
VO:
Yashini Padayachee is a South African born television presenter working for TRT World in Türkiye. She lives in Istanbul, a city that was not affected by the Earthquakes. She witnessed the tragedy unfold, together with millions of viewers.
Yashni: It was almost 10 hours later, that there was a second earthquake, and this I think was a 7.5 Magnitude earthquake, and this is something you just do not hear of
Prof.
Türkiye is on this region that Geophysicists call Anatolia, and it is being squeezed in between Arabia and Eurasia.
VO: Professor Raymond Durrheim, teaches Geosciences at the University of the Witwatersrand. He is part of a group researching, Earthquakes and Seismology; they have been following the disaster in Syria and Türkiye.
Prof
Why did this happen? Well, this is just part of a long natural process of the continents moving around and jostling with each other. In that part of the world there are earthquakes you could say virtually daily. Maybe every decade or two, there would be a destructive earthquake, and perhaps every century or two, there would be a great earthquake like this, that causes widespread damage.
Yahini:
You know you don't have to be somebody was living here you just have to be a human being but we can look at the children who have not made it the parents were searching for their children families that have been completely separated in the middle of winter in what people have described as the worst disaster to hit that care in a century.
Dr Bahm:
We've seen people just sit and a side of the street lost and just trying to see what is happen
Dr Ahmed Bahm, is the Head of Gift of the Givers, a disaster response organisation from South Africa. His team is currently in Türkiye, providing assistance.
Dr Bahm:
Most of the injuries that we are currently seeing, is traumatic huge cuts or amputations and Crush injuries and that's the type of Injuries that we are currently seeing.
VO:
As is often the case with tragedies, hope is what brings us together. In a war torn Syria, a voluntary group called “The White Helmets” are working around the clock to save lives. For now at least, the sound of guns is replaced by silence, as they listen for signs of life.
Yashini:
Seeing stories of babies being pulled out alive have been particularly heart-warming. There was a story in Syria of a woman who gave birth under the Rubble, she sadly didn't survive but her newborn infant did! And was pulled out by rescue workers. That baby has been born in the midst of Tragedy but is already a survivor.
The Turkish citizens have been so warm welcoming , praising you, motivating you and just saying thank you for coming thank you South Africa you came all the way from South Africa to be with us.
VO: For people like Fatih, far removed from the chaos, it is just as difficult. Grateful that his family is safe in Türkiye, he knows every day he is able to talk to them is a blessing.


Fatih:
Turkish people, are good people and they are gonna, they gonna help them, they gonna help each other they Gonna sort it out what is not easy.
Yashini:
That is very much a Turkish sentiment that the country that comes together in times of need and that type of strength and unity and resilience is definitely going to be needed over the long term.



PROMO ONE


Opening shot buildings flattened…


UPSOUND news clip: “… breaking news...an earthquake on a terrifying scale… {wait two beats]”


VO: Multiple devastating earthquakes… the race to find survivors… {viz and audio from rescue operation }


VO: …. and the power of the human spirit…
UPSOUND Yashini … It’s a country that comes together ….and that type of resilience is definitely going to be needed over the long term…




PROMO TWO


From your current cut


02:29 - 02:55 - Yashini “You don’t have to be…” - you’ll just need to trim 5 seconds off to get it to 21 but it’s pretty powerful.




PROMO THREE
VO: In Turkiye and Syria… the search for survivors is still on…
UPSOUND: Most of the injuries that we’re seeing is traumatic, huge cuts, amputaions…
VO: And as rescue turns to recovery, Gift of the givers is lending a helping hand…

Title Author Last Updated 12 February 2023 - Carte Blanche HD nombuso@carteblanche.co.za 13 February 2023 TX Date: 0000-00-00 Script: Opening: Clips from social media, chaos, devastation, up-sounds… VO: In the early hours of Monday morning, multiple deadly earthquakes, rocked Syria and Türkiye . It’s a tragedy that struck thousands of kms away. But, even here, in a suburban restaurant in Sunninghill Johannesburg, popular with locals and expats, the aftershocks are being felt... Fatih: When I woke up, I saw the news, tried to phone someone, they did not answer… I texted using whatsapp… Maybe they died, maybe they are still alive, some of them. VO: Fatih grew up in Türkiye, but moved to Joburg to run his restaurant, Istanbul Kebab. Following the disaster, he was desperately trying to get hold of his family back home, but to no avail. Then, hours later, came the good news… they were unharmed. Fatih: I can't tell you, you have to be there, we can see what's happening there. We are sad for other people! They lose their family and everything, actually. According to reports, 23 million people have been affected by these earthquakes. However, this is not a new phenomenon. Earthquakes are a common occurrence in the region. Yashni: It was a 7.7 Magnitude earthquake, that is massive. That happened in the early hours of the morning, just after 4 O'clock. VO: Yashini Padayachee is a South African born television presenter working for TRT World in Türkiye. She lives in Istanbul, a city that was not affected by the Earthquakes. She witnessed the tragedy unfold, together with millions of viewers. Yashni: It was almost 10 hours later, that there was a second earthquake, and this I think was a 7.5 Magnitude earthquake, and this is something you just do not hear of Prof. Türkiye is on this region that Geophysicists call Anatolia, and it is being squeezed in between Arabia and Eurasia. VO: Professor Raymond Durrheim, teaches Geosciences at the University of the Witwatersrand. He is part of a group researching, Earthquakes and Seismology; they have been following the disaster in Syria and Türkiye. Prof Why did this happen? Well, this is just part of a long natural process of the continents moving around and jostling with each other. In that part of the world there are earthquakes you could say virtually daily. Maybe every decade or two, there would be a destructive earthquake, and perhaps every century or two, there would be a great earthquake like this, that causes widespread damage. Yahini: You know you don't have to be somebody was living here you just have to be a human being but we can look at the children who have not made it the parents were searching for their children families that have been completely separated in the middle of winter in what people have described as the worst disaster to hit that care in a century. Dr Bahm: We've seen people just sit and a side of the street lost and just trying to see what is happen Dr Ahmed Bahm, is the Head of Gift of the Givers, a disaster response organisation from South Africa. His team is currently in Türkiye, providing assistance. Dr Bahm: Most of the injuries that we are currently seeing, is traumatic huge cuts or amputations and Crush injuries and that's the type of Injuries that we are currently seeing. VO: As is often the case with tragedies, hope is what brings us together. In a war torn Syria, a voluntary group called “The White Helmets” are working around the clock to save lives. For now at least, the sound of guns is replaced by silence, as they listen for signs of life. Yashini: Seeing stories of babies being pulled out alive have been particularly heart-warming. There was a story in Syria of a woman who gave birth under the Rubble, she sadly didn't survive but her newborn infant did! And was pulled out by rescue workers. That baby has been born in the midst of Tragedy but is already a survivor. The Turkish citizens have been so warm welcoming , praising you, motivating you and just saying thank you for coming thank you South Africa you came all the way from South Africa to be with us. VO: For people like Fatih, far removed from the chaos, it is just as difficult. Grateful that his family is safe in Türkiye, he knows every day he is able to talk to them is a blessing. Fatih: Turkish people, are good people and they are gonna, they gonna help them, they gonna help each other they Gonna sort it out what is not easy. Yashini: That is very much a Turkish sentiment that the country that comes together in times of need and that type of strength and unity and resilience is definitely going to be needed over the long term. PROMO ONE Opening shot buildings flattened… UPSOUND news clip: “… breaking news...an earthquake on a terrifying scale… {wait two beats]” VO: Multiple devastating earthquakes… the race to find survivors… {viz and audio from rescue operation } VO: …. and the power of the human spirit… UPSOUND Yashini … It’s a country that comes together ….and that type of resilience is definitely going to be needed over the long term… PROMO TWO From your current cut 02:29 - 02:55 - Yashini “You don’t have to be…” - you’ll just need to trim 5 seconds off to get it to 21 but it’s pretty powerful. PROMO THREE VO: In Turkiye and Syria… the search for survivors is still on… UPSOUND: Most of the injuries that we’re seeing is traumatic, huge cuts, amputaions… VO: And as rescue turns to recovery, Gift of the givers is lending a helping hand…

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): ... in the aftermath of the devastating earthquakes in Turkiye and Syria, we take you inside the unfolding tragedy.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Turkey and Syria earthquake - the death toll passes 11,000.
